one_liner: Compact Rust Wasm runtime whose single-pass AArch64 compiler compiles faster than wasmtime Winch and wasmer Singlepass.
what_it_does: wisp is a Rust library and CLI (wisp run, validate, inspect, compile) that decodes, validates and runs WebAssembly 2.0 core modules without SIMD, with WASI preview 1. The embedding API follows wasmtime's shape (Engine, Module, Store, Instance, Linker, Caller, func.call with a slice of Val), so porting embedder code is mostly renaming, but it is not a drop-in replacement. Engine::default uses the baseline compiler on AArch64 macOS and the interpreter everywhere else; fuel metering is optional.
how_it_is_fast: Compile speed comes from a Liftoff-style single-pass compiler with no IR: an abstract operand stack whose entries sit in a register, a spill slot, the condition flags (so i32.lt_s; br_if becomes cmp; b.lt) or a pending constant, emitted straight through its own AArch64 encoder into MAP_JIT memory. Everything is spilled at block boundaries, so merges need no reconciliation; that keeps compilation cheap (the README demo compiles 1.36 MB regex.wasm in 8.3 ms in-process) but costs run-time speed. The interpreter uses slot-addressed three-address bytecode (the operand at depth d lives in slot nlocals+d), fused compare-and-branch and callee frames laid over the caller's argument slots.
when_to_use: Short-lived, compile-dominated Wasm runs on Apple Silicon macOS, where compile latency matters more than peak throughput (regex.wasm compile-only 16.3 ms against 24.2 ms for Winch and 31.5 ms for Singlepass).
Mid-sized programs where a baseline compiler is enough: whole-process time beats wasmtime Winch on fib, raytrace, json and regex.
Studying or teaching how a complete Wasm engine is built: about 12,600 lines with a design document, its own spec runner and a wasm-smith differential fuzzer.
A dependency-light Rust embedding (libc is the only runtime dependency) that needs a cap-std-style WASI path sandbox.
when_not_to_use: Throughput-bound work: end to end it is 1.5-2.5x slower than wasmtime Cranelift on six of seven programs, and slower than Winch on primes (0.120 s vs 0.070 s), matmul and compress.
Linux, x86-64 or Windows hosts: the compiler runs only on AArch64 macOS (Linux AArch64 paths exist but are disabled), and the interpreter used elsewhere is 3-8x slower than the compiler.
Modules that need SIMD (v128 is rejected), threads, or any Wasm 3.0 feature (GC, exceptions, tail calls, memory64, multi-memory).
C or C++ hosts: there is no C API header yet.
Production use: 15 commits made on 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-02, version 0.1.0 unreleased, 0 stars, one author, no outside users or issues.

integration.form: crate (use a git dependency; the crates.io name 'wisp' belongs to an unrelated tmux tool) plus a CLI binary
integration.dependencies: libc only; wast and wat are dev-dependencies for the spec runner; the spec suite is downloaded with curl on first test run
integration.platforms: compiler: AArch64 macOS only; interpreter: any host Rust targets (CI runs macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64)
integration.thread_safety: a Store is single-threaded; handles (Func, Memory and so on) are plain indices not checked against the Store they came from
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — API resembles wasmtime's but types and crate differ; no SIMD, threads or Wasm 3.0, and the compiler only on macOS AArch64

gotchas: Compile-time comparison is not like for like: every figure is whole-process wall clock including start-up, wisp compile keeps the code in memory and compiles on one thread, while wasmtime compile and wasmer compile run in parallel and also serialize and write an artefact to disk. The README demo shows 8.3 ms of actual compile inside wisp's 13.7 ms in-process total for regex.wasm.

The end-to-end rows under about 0.06 s (fib, matmul, raytrace) are dominated by process start-up and compilation, so wins over Winch there partly reflect wisp's faster compile rather than better generated code; the fib win over Cranelift (0.022 s vs 0.024 s) is within the noise of 5 runs on a machine shared with other work.
Linear-memory accesses carry an explicit add; cmp; b.hi bounds check (no guard pages); the design notes blame it for the 2.5x gap to wasmtime on the memory-bound sieve.

Functions too large for the 1 MiB reach of AArch64 conditional branches are silently left to the interpreter (a performance cliff on very large functions), and fuel traps may fire up to one block early.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick wisp over zwasm or cataggar/wamr only when you want a small, readable Rust engine with a baseline compiler on Apple Silicon and value compile latency; for a portable Rust embedding with fast startup pick Wasmi, and for throughput stay on wasmtime Cranelift.
verified_claims_summary: First-party bench/run.py on an Apple M5 (10 cores, macOS 27, shared with other work) compares wisp 0.1.0 with wasmtime 49.0.1 and wasmer 7.5.0 release binaries with caches off, taking the median of 5 whole-process wall-clock runs and checking each run's output against native. Compile-only for regex.wasm takes 16.3 ms for wisp against 24.2 ms (Winch), 31.5 ms (Singlepass), 71.6 ms (wasmtime Cranelift) and 82.0 ms (wasmer Cranelift). End to end, wisp beats Winch on 4 of 7 programs but trails Cranelift by 1.5-2.5x on 6 of 7. The rustc version of the measured build is not recorded.
status_note: Brand-new single-author project (15 commits over two days in October 2026, 0.1.0 unreleased) that is MIT-licensed and small enough to read or vendor, but it is a study piece, not yet a production runtime.
